study.title: Proverbs 29 - Discipline, government and the two paths
study.overview: Proverbs 29 gathers sayings that show how the human response to correction, the quality of leadership, the use of the word and the disposition of the heart shape both personal life and public life. The chapter opposes the stubborn to the teachable, the righteous to the wicked, the wise to the rash and the humble to the arrogant. It also insists that social order depends not only on human force: the Lord judges, sustains and gives direction. The end of the chapter closes with a strong moral thesis: there is a real enmity between justice and perversity, and this appears in the attitudes of both sides.

outline.title: Weathern, justice and moral influence
outline.explanation: The first proverbs show the end of the person who rejects repeated warnings, the impact that righteous or perverse rulers exert on the people, and as personal choices - wisdom, prostitution, bajulation and transgression - bring joy, ruin or traps.

outline.title: The righteous defend, the wise contain anger, and discipline teaches
outline.explanation: This section contrasts the righteous one who considers the cause of the poor with the wicked who does not understand this; highlights the peacemaking power of the wise man, the hostility of the violent against the righteous, the self-control of the wise, the corruption produced by lies in the government and the value of correction to form children and rulers.

outline.title: Without direction, the people are confused; speech and disorderly anger multiply evil
outline.explanation: Here arises the social effects of the multiplication of the perverses, the need for prophetic vision and to keep the law, the limitation of mere words to correct certain servants, the danger of responding with precipitation, the reckless indulgence with subordinates and the damage of easy wrath and wrath.

outline.title: Humility, man's fear and the conflict between two types of people
outline.explanation: The final passage teaches that the pride overthrows, humility honor, complicity with the thief destroys one's own life, the fear of people creates bonds of fear, the Lord is the final judge and, finally, just and perverses if they hate each other because they follow opposite paths.

study.context: The chapter belongs to the Sapiential Collection of Proverbs and brings together short, practical and moral observations about family life, leadership, justice and social coexistence. The text does not present a continuous narrative; it alternates applications about the king, the father, the servant, the fool, the just and the wicked. The notes received reinforce that the chapter speaks of discipline, integrity government, self-control and fear of the Lord, without requiring historical reconstructions beyond what the text itself affirms.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that biblical wisdom is not only intellectual: it appears in self-control, in submission to correction, in the defense of the poor, in the refusal of lies and trust in the Lord. Human authority is real, but limited; the righteous king preserves the command while the Lord is the decisive judge of all. The discipline is presented as an instrument of formation, not as mere punishment. The text also treats ethics as something relational: the just not only avoids evil, but opposes the wicked, and this opposition reveals that there are two ways of walking in the world. In Protestant evangelical key, this harmonizes with the need for a transformed heart: without inner change, external correction, law and leadership do not solve the fundamental problem of sin.

scholarViews.insight: The control of emotions is a mark of wisdom: the prudent person remains calm even under pressure, in contrast to impulsiveness.
The righteous do not silence himself before evil; he wants the good of his neighbor and even the enemies, while the violent hate the righteous because they testify against wickedness.
The hatred between wicked and upright expresses deep contrariety between the two paths; Clarke also understands that the "path" of the verse points to the right conduct and to the divine word kept.

questions: In which areas of my life have I received repeated correction, but I continue to harden the heart?
Do my speech and my temperament promote peace and justice, or multiply contention and transgressions?
How can I trust the Lord more than in the fear of people and at the same time act with courage and integrity?
study.practice: Practice the wisdom of this chapter on three fronts: receive correction without resistance, especially when it comes from reliable people; examine your posture before authorities, subordinates and poor, so as not to use power, word or influence unfairly; discipline and your mouth and your emotions, avoiding precipitation, bajulation, easy anger and complicity with error. In family and community life, treat discipline as loving care and not as humiliation. Finally, consciously choose the path of the righteous, even if this generates opposition, because the text states that the final judgment belongs to the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The text provided is in Portuguese and some expressions are paraphrastic; therefore, the analysis depends on the writing presented, not on a critical comparison with the original Hebrew. The commentator notes were used only as interpretive voices and, in some verses, they add nuances that should not be treated as indisputable conclusions of the text. There is no basis for the scores to make detailed historical data, dates, locations or reconstruction archaeological reconstruction.
